title: Is building a new stadium a way around spending rules?
description: Spurs only just avoided Premier League relegation last season, but off the pitch they are thriving. So is building a new stadium a good way around spending rules?
fullText:
Tottenham fans will want to put last season behind them.

There was another managerial sacking, a spate of injuries to key players, and a nervy 90 minutes on the final day of the season as the ninth-richest club in the world, external narrowly avoided relegation from the Premier League.

A 17th-place finish for the second year running will be cause for concern, to say the least.

Off the pitch though it's a different story. Tottenham's finances, despite the team's poor form, are looking very rosy indeed. This is largely down to their new stadium and the huge revenues it brings.

So what can other clubs learn from their stadium success story? And is building a new home - or renovating an old one - the best way to balance the books?

We'll get to complying with financial rules in a moment, but first let's start by looking at how much a club like Tottenham are making on matchdays.

"Spurs' matchday income has increased from £45m in 2016-17, the season they left White Hart Lane, to £126m in 2024-25," explains football finance expert Kieran Maguire.

"So you've less than doubled the size of the stadium and yet the matchday revenue is up by two and a half times.

"What Spurs have done is they've created a welcoming environment. So if people are spending an extra 40 to 50 minutes in the stadium itself they're not just spending time - more importantly they're spending money."

Spurs can also host up to 30 non-football events a year at full capacity which is proving to be very beneficial.

Along with major concerts, the club has also hosted NFL games and boxing world title fights - including Anthony Joshua's heavyweight bout with Oleksandr Usyk in 2021. It's also been the venue for rugby union's Saracens hosting Harlequins in the London derby since 2023.

All of this brings in extra commercial revenue - which jumped from £73m in 2016-17 to £277m in 2024-25.

The extra income means the club can then invest 

This summer the Premier League is replacing its profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) with a new financial framework centred on squad-cost ratio (SCR) and sustainability and systemic resilience (SSR).

Put simply, SCR is designed to cap a club's total spending on its playing squad as a direct percentage of its overall revenue.

Club costs like player wages, transfer amortisation - spreading a transfer fee across the length of a player's contract for accounting purposes - and agent fees all get taken into account.

Crucially though, stadium infrastructure costs are not included in the SCR calculation.

"In the case of Spurs, their infrastructure costs are around £70m a year - but those are excluded." says Maguire. "Any money that you invest in stadiums is completely ring-fenced and excluded from your ability to invest in players.

"There's a separate issue in that stadiums do cost a lot of money. But Spurs borrowed from banks at spectacularly cheap interest rates."

In other words, for Spurs the pluses of building a new expensive stadium far outweigh the negatives, at least from a financial perspective.

"In order to be competitive, you need to have a significant increase in matchday income," says Maguire.

"You could only do that from either increasing prices, which isn't going to go down well, or increasing the size of the stadium with a greater proportion of the tickets going to the non-season ticket fanbase."

Like Tottenham, Everton and West Ham have also moved to new stadiums - which while financially attractive in the long-term, hasn't always gone down well with fans.

Other Premier League clubs are looking at their options. Should they stay or go?

Renovation is the cheaper route, but the problem then is where do the team play if they have to move out while building takes place?

The obvious barrier to moving to a new stadium is the huge cost - but there's also the concern from fans that they'll lose something by leaving their historical home.

It is clear Sir Jim Ratcliffe wants a new stadium to be the statement around his involvement at Manchester United.

Yet it is equally clear a new build, with a 100,000 capacity and a significant number of corporate areas, would generate far more than United get on a matchday now, which will help drive revenues and improve the senior squad.

There are other financial aspects though, which few will consider in the bigger picture.

The initial plans unveiled by Ratcliffe in March 2025 featured a huge canopy. That in itself will be costly, but in theory the overhang and what is underneath it will be in United's footprint - and the club will be responsible for it. Will the expense be worth the 'look'?

Construction could - in part - take place off site and be shipped in if club officials are to be believed. That is likely to cost less than doing all the work in Old Trafford.

And then having a new build where it is, down the road from their current ground, deals with the potentially thorny problem about where United would play if Old Trafford was closed for a period.

None of Manchester City, Liverpool or Everton's grounds are ideal from a security perspective. All have a lower capacity than Old Trafford and all would cost a lot to hire, even if it was desirable.

United's current plans mean they can simply move from one stadium to another.

For Newcastle, a club which this summer has effectively had to sell some of its best players in order to stay within the financial rules, the argument over moving to a new purpose-built stadium is compelling.

"For the 2024-25 season Newcastle's matchday income was £52m. Manchester United's was £160m, Arsenal's £154m, Spurs' was £126m.

"If you're £100m behind your competitors, the only way to address that is either to be super smart or to charge more money for the product.

"How can Newcastle increase the yield per fan and still be loyal to the Gallowgate hardcore? You need to be able to offer a different product and St James' Park wasn't built for a corporate audience."

Will the fans back a move though?

Newcastle supporter Charlotte Robson has mixed feelings.

"I think we can host gigs at St James' Park but probably not on the scale of Spurs or West Ham's London Stadium.

"I don't think it would be stupid to move from the ground but I think there is so much identity for Newcastle fans who are attached to St James' Park that it would break a lot of hearts to move the ground in any significant way."

title: The Premier League clubs fighting a World Cup hangover
description: Which Premier League clubs have carried the biggest World Cup workload?
fullText:
The Premier League season begins on 21 August - just 33 days after the World Cup final.

For some clubs, that leaves barely enough time to welcome players back from the mandatory three-week post-tournament break required under Fifa regulations, let alone integrate them into pre-season preparations.

Four Tottenham players were still involved on the final weekend of the tournament and may have little more than a week of training before the new campaign starts. Chelsea too were significantly affected.

And Manchester City and Arsenal have their own concerns after seeing more players than any other Premier League club reach the latter stages of the competition.

The World Cup may be over, but its impact on the Premier League is only just beginning.

Tottenham are among the clubs whose pre-season preparations have been most significantly impacted.

Cristian Romero and new signing Marcos Senesi reached the final with Argentina, while Pedro Porro helped Spain lift the trophy. Djed Spence remained with England until the third-place play-off on 18 July.

Assuming players take the minimum three weeks off under Fifa guidelines, the players who reached the final would not return until 9 August, while Spence's earliest return date would be 8 August.

That leaves them with around two weeks to reintegrate before their Premier League season begins at Brentford on 22 August.

However, Spurs confirmed that Senesi - who made two World Cup appearances after being a late call-up for Argentina - was at the club's training ground for the first time on Thursday for pre-season testing.

For managers, the challenge is not simply the absence itself. Players returning so late miss much of pre-season's tactical work, conditioning sessions and friendly matches, creating a difficult balancing act between preparation and recovery.

Manchester City and Arsenal, meanwhile, had the greatest concentration of players making deep runs into the competition.

City's World Cup contingent featured for several of the tournament's leading nations.

Rodri helped Spain win their second men's World Cup after playing 726 minutes, while Marc Guehi and Elliot Anderson helped England reach the final weekend.

Nico O'Reilly featured in England's semi-final run, while Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku both reached the quarter-finals.

Arsenal's numbers were similarly striking.

Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka remained involved until England's 6-4 victory over France in the third-place play-off, while Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino reached the final with Spain.

William Saliba helped France reach the third-place play-off, although he was subsequently injured and did not feature again. Noni Madueke was part of England's run to the final weekend but did not play beyond the quarter-finals, while Martin Odegaard captained Norway to the quarter-finals.

The workload concerns are already being felt. City's Rodri recently had back surgery and is expected to miss a "short period" at the start of the season, while Saliba avoided surgery, but Arsenal have confirmed he will be sidelined for an "extended period" because of a back issue.

Even though neither setback can be attributed solely to the World Cup, both underline the physical demands being placed on players in an increasingly crowded football calendar.

Those clubs are likely to begin the campaign without having enjoyed a full pre-season with several key players.

The World Cup's biggest workload belonged to Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who played all 810 minutes of Argentina's run to the final.

Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister ranked second among Premier League players with 749 minutes, while Spain midfielder Rodri was third on 726.

Several players effectively completed the equivalent of eight full matches during the tournament.

Goalkeepers naturally face different physical demands from outfield players, but the figures underline the extent of Premier League involvement throughout the competition.

With the players entitled to a minimum three-week break under Fifa regulations, for those involved in the final on 19 July - including Rodri, Porro, Zubimendi, Mac Allister, Enzo Fernandez, Emiliano Martinez and Lisandro Martinez - the earliest return date is 9 August.

Players who featured in England's third-place play-off will return a day earlier.

That leaves clubs with roughly 12 days to reintegrate some of their most important players before competitive football begins.

The concerns extend beyond this summer's World Cup.

Many of football's leading players have now experienced three consecutive summers of major tournaments, following Euro 2024 and Copa America, then last year's expanded Club World Cup and now the World Cup.

One of those players is Rodri, who warned in 2024 that footballers were "close" to striking because of workload concerns.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca have also voiced concerns about the demands being placed on elite players and the growing number of matches in the calendar.

The growing injury list during the World Cup provided another reminder of those concerns.

Aston Villa midfielder Amadou Onana suffered a serious knee injury while representing Belgium, while Manchester United and Uruguay defensive midfielder Manuel Ugarte saw his tournament cut short by injury. Reece James also had his minutes carefully managed by England as he continued his recovery from a hamstring problem.

For clubs such as Tottenham, Arsenal, Manchester City and Chelsea, the challenge is now immediate.

The World Cup has concluded. The countdown to the Premier League season is under way.

But for some players, recovery comes first, and the race to be ready for opening weekend has only just begun.

title: 22 needed off 6: Ex-CSK star Vijay Shankar's batting ends in wicket-maiden as Dilshan Madushanka seals last-over win in LPL
description: The Lanka Premier League continues to be one of the most thrilling T20 leagues as Vijay Shankar's shocking batting in the final over ends with a wicket-maiden and defeat.
fullText:
22 needed off 6: Ex-CSK star Vijay Shankar's batting ends in wicket-maiden as Dilshan Madushanka seals last-over win in LPL originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Dilshan Madushanka bowled a final-over wicket maiden to seal Jaffna Kings' win in LPL 2026.

Kandy Royals needed 22 off the last six balls with one recognised batter left.

Former CSK star Vijay Shankar was dismissed off the final delivery as Kandy fell 21 short.

The Lanka Premier League served up a gripping finish in Pallekele on Thursday, with a title contender's chase collapsing at the last hurdle. What had been a high-scoring contest between Jaffna Kings and Kandy Royals came down to a single, unforgettable over from a Sri Lanka international.

Batting first after being invited to do so, Jaffna posted an imposing 221/6, built on brisk contributions through their order. As reported by NDTV, Kamil Mishara top-scored with 49 while Chamindu Wickramasinghe provided late impetus with 43 off just 15 balls, setting Kandy a daunting target.

Kandy Royals mounted a spirited response but ultimately fell short, bowled out for 200 to lose by 21 runs. The chase never quite kept pace with the rate, and the equation grew steeper as wickets tumbled around a series of promising starts.

MORE: Jamie George and Owen Farrell to take on Somerset cricket stars in charity T20 match

The decisive drama unfolded in the 20th over, with Kandy requiring 22 runs from six balls and clinging to their last recognised batter. Left-arm quick Dilshan Madushanka was handed the ball against former India batter Vijay Shankar, and he responded with a spell of ruthless precision.

According to ESPNcricinfo's commentary, Madushanka speared in a mix of slower off-cutters and yorkers that left Shankar swinging in vain. Five successive dot balls followed, the batter unable to make clean contact, before Madushanka rounded off the wicket-maiden by dismissing Shankar off the final delivery to seal victory in style.

Shankar, who had earlier fought to 25 off 21 balls, could only pull the last ball to deep backward square leg, ending both the innings and Kandy's hopes. The win lifted Jaffna to the top of the points table.

MORE: 'Simply no match for him': Amir names Virat as the toughest to bowl

The foundation for Jaffna's defence was laid long before the final over. As reported by NDTV, Dunith Wellalage swung the contest firmly in the Kings' favour with an outstanding spell of 3/11, choking Kandy's momentum through the middle overs.

He found able support across the attack. Shakib Al Hasan chipped in with important wickets, while Kandy's brightest resistance came from Pawan Sandesh, whose quick-fire 48 from 21 deliveries briefly threatened before the asking rate spiralled beyond their reach.

For Kandy, two wickets apiece from Wanindu Hasaranga and Moeen Ali had kept Jaffna's total within reach, but the batting could not finish the job. Jaffna Kings will now face Dambulla Sixers on Sunday in their final league fixture.

MORE: Sammy vs Joseph: What happened as WI pacer drops 'not representing Sammy' bombshell

The margin of 21 runs and the theatre of the last over should not disguise what was, in truth, a comfortable Jaffna win. Kandy's chase flickered without ever genuinely threatening, and needing 22 off the final six with one wicket standing was less a nail-biter than a formality dressed up as tension.

The lasting image, though, belongs to Madushanka, whose ice-cold execution under the lights offered a reminder of his international pedigree. For Shankar and Kandy, it was a deflating way to surrender a contest, their playoff hopes fraying further with each dot ball of an over they would want to forget.

title: England's Stones joins Inter Milan on free transfer
description: England centre-back John Stones has joined Inter Milan on a free transfer after spending 10 years with Manchester City, the Italian champions announced on Thursday.Stones was a key player for Manchester City during their golden era under former manager Pep Guardiola, winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League crown with the club.
fullText:
England centre-back John Stones has joined Inter Milan on a free transfer after spending 10 years with Manchester City, the Italian champions announced on Thursday.

The 32-year-old left City when his contract expired at the end of last month, while playing for England at the World Cup where he helped them to a third-placed finish.

Stones has signed a two-year deal with Inter, a club statement said.

He played five times for England at the recent World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada, making his 94th international appearance in the semi-final loss to Argentina.

Stones was a key player for Manchester City during their golden era under former manager Pep Guardiola, winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League crown with the club.

His final few seasons at the Etihad Stadium, though, were hit by injuries, and he only made nine Premier League appearances last term.

Stones could make his Inter debut when they start their Scudetto defence against Monza at the San Siro on August 22.

title: Premier League clubs agree EFL funding proposal
description: Premier League clubs agreed a funding proposal that they will put to the EFL over the next few days.
fullText:
An end is finally in sight to the long-running funding dispute between the Premier League and the English Football League.

The Premier League confirmed its 20 clubs have "unanimously voted" to approve a proposal for a "new strategic partnership", which will be put to the EFL for its members to vote on in the next few days.

No figure has been put on the deal, which is due to last 10 years, with both sides keen not to debate the issue in public.

The Premier League says the proposal is fully funded. It is expected to come through a transfer levy.

"The Premier League already has long-term funding commitments to invest a record £1.6billion every three years into the wider game and communities," said the Premier League.

"The Premier League remains committed to finding a football-led solution and looks forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal."

'Clock ticking' on financial stand-off - regulator

The funding row has been rumbling on since a fan-led review in 2021, which was commissioned by the government following a number of crises in the sport, including the failed European Super League project and the collapse of Bury FC.

On a number of occasions, it has seemed a deal was close. In March 2024, the Premier League was warned by government officials that if it and the EFL failed to agree a deal, one would be imposed on them.

On Tuesday, representatives of the Premier League, the EFL and the new Independent Regulator met to discuss the outline of a deal.

"The EFL notes the Premier League's position following its meeting with clubs earlier today, and now looks forward to receiving its formal proposal for consideration," said the EFL.

"This follows constructive discussions involving the EFL, Premier League and Independent Football Regulator over recent months.

"The EFL Board will then review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League.

"The proposal will then be discussed in detail with our member clubs to determine next steps."

Resistance within the Premier League simply to hand over money was based on a number of factors, including the basic reality they would providing funds to clubs trying to replace them.

In other instances, specifically Stoke City, EFL clubs have owners richer than some in the Premier League.

title: Wrexham eager to chart a pathway to the Premier League next season
description: Wrexham will head into the 2026/27 Championship season as one of the favourites to win promotion to the Premier League.Some impressive pre-season performances have raised expectations around a club wh...
fullText:
Wrexham will head into the 2026/27 Championship season as one of the favourites to win promotion to the Premier League.

Some impressive pre-season performances have raised expectations around a club which has enjoyed a meteoric rise in recent years.

After drawing with Wisla Krakow (0-0), the Welsh club recorded victories over Manchester United (1-0) and Leeds United (3-2).

A narrow 1-0 defeat against Liverpool at Yankee Stadium in New York failed to dampen enthusiasm around the club.

Wrexham have undoubtedly come a long way since co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney completed their purchase of the club in 2021.

Their investment has helped the Dragons climb from the National League to the Championship. They are just one promotion away from the top flight.

Manager Phil Parkinson is now eager to complete the journey. He believes their pre-season results highlight the progress they have made.

“You play Man United, Leeds and Liverpool and you come away with a single-goal defeat as your worst result out of the three, you have to say that’s not a bad result,” he said.

“In terms of the performance, we’re learning as a team. When we’re under a little bit of pressure and we get the ball back, that’s when we have to lift the game and give ourselves a breather with the ball.

“When we did that, I thought we did okay.”

Wrexham kicked off their summer transfer business with the signing of wing-back Danny Imray from Crystal Palace for an undisclosed fee.

The 23-year-old spent the second half of last season on loan at West Bromwich Albion and produced a series of impressive performances.

More new signings are expected at Wrexham, with the co-owners willing to sanction another major spending spree this summer.

Sunderland goalkeeper Anthony Patterson and Everton shot-stopper Mark Travers are potential transfer targets.

Leicester City defender Harry Souttar has also been linked with the club, although the £10m asking price is a stumbling block.

Senegal forward Bamba Dieng has been touted as a possible option, but a move for Portsmouth defender Terry Devlin is unlikely following the Imray deal.

More potential targets will emerge during August as Wrexham strive to win promotion to the Premier League at the second time of asking.

Wrexham agonisingly missed out on the play-offs last term as they finished two points behind Hull City, who subsequently went on to win the play-off final.

The English Football League’s decision to expand the Championship play-offs from four teams to six should work to Wrexham’s advantage.

West Ham United and Wolverhampton Wanderers are expected to be in contention for automatic promotion following their relegation from the top flight.

Burnley, Middlesbrough and Birmingham City are other clubs who will expect to be challenging for a top two spot.

Wrexham’s investment in their squad could bring them into the equation, although a place in the expanded play-offs is a more likely target.

Sheffield United, Norwich City and Derby County are amongst a plethora of clubs who will be eyeing a top eight finish.

If Wrexham can spend their transfer kitty wisely, there is no reason why they can’t mount a sustained challenge for promotion.

However, given the strength of the Championship this season, it would be foolish to think the outcome is a foregone conclusion.

title: Four pointers to most open Premier League title race in years
description: Three of the Premier League's "big six" have new managers, the champions have a key injury issue and Tottenham and Chelsea are breaking transfer records - and that might mean a very open title race.
fullText:
Three of the traditional "big six" have new managers, the defending champions have a key injury and Tottenham and Chelsea are breaking transfer records.

After years of Manchester City dominance followed by Liverpool and Arsenal winning titles by at least seven points, the Premier League is due a wide open, unpredictable, multi-club title race.

Here are four reasons why 2026-27 could be that season.

How do you replace the irreplaceable?

Manchester City are often title favourites having won six of the past nine Premier League trophies, but they start this new season without their greatest ever manager, Pep Guardiola.

The 55-year-old led City to 17 major trophies in 10 years, but left at the end of last season and has since been replaced by his former assistant Enzo Maresca.

Maresca has been out of work since stepping down as Chelsea boss in January.

The Blues also have a new gaffer. They replaced Maresca with Liam Rosenior in January but he was let go before the end of the season and now former Liverpool player Xabi Alonso is at the helm.

Alonso won the Bundesliga with an invincible Bayer Leverkusen team two years ago but last term had a difficult spell in charge of Real Madrid.

Many thought he would replace 2024-25 title-winner Arne Slot at Liverpool but the Reds instead have appointed Andoni Iraola, who finished sixth with Bournemouth last season.

That's three huge clubs with three new managers.

What's more, Manchester United's Michael Carrick and Tottenham's Roberto de Zerbi only took charge part way through last season.

So five of the traditional big six will start to the new campaign with a different manager to the one they had at the start of last season.

Only Mikel Arteta of Arsenal, appointed in 2019, remains.

As defending champions and with an experienced manager, Arsenal are favourites for the Premier League title.

But a lengthy injury to a key starter could affect their title chances.

The club have said defender William Saliba is set to miss an "extended period" after suffering a back injury while at the World Cup with France.

Saliba, 25, made 50 appearances in all competitions for Arsenal last season and his formidable partnership with team-mate Gabriel was a big factor in them conceding fewer goals than anyone else in the division.

Arsenal have a tricky start to the season, facing Aston Villa and Chelsea in two of their first three matches.

Since Saliba's debut in 2022, Arsenal have won 68.7% of their Premier League matches when he has been in the team (131 games).

When he has been sidelined, that win percentage drops to 47.6% (21 games).

Last season, Manchester United played just 40 matches in all competitions, their fewest in a single campaign since 1914-15, and finished third.

Chelsea played 59 matches in all competitions and finished 10th.

Tottenham played 52 matches in all competitions and avoided relegation on the final day, finishing 17th.

Playing more matches does not always correlate with a lower league finish. Arsenal, for instance, won the Premier League title last season while reaching both the Champions League and Carabao Cup finals.

But fewer matches in other competitions does mean a team can rotate less, often have a full week of preparation between games and be less susceptible to injuries.

Spurs had a staggering 27 different players sidelined at some point last season.

Next season Chelsea and Tottenham are not playing European football whereas Manchester United and eight other Premier League clubs are.

United have responded by targeting midfielders in the transfer market, having bought Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans from Chelsea and Aston Villa respectfully.

But will those two additions be enough to cover the club's increased workload?

Chelsea and Tottenham both underperformed last season, but the pair could pick up this term after going big in the transfer window.

Chelsea made England midfielder Morgan Rogers the most expensive British player in history this month by signing him from Aston Villa for a fee of £117m.

They've also spent £47m on full-back Marco Palestra from Atalanta and are close to deals for Danny Welbeck, Jordan Henderson and Maxence Lacroix.

Tottenham have almost matched Chelsea's spending, parting with a club record £237m this summer.

In July, Spurs broke their transfer record twice in two days, first signing midfielder Mateus Fernandes from West Ham for £85m before bringing in Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m.

They've also picked up Jan Paul van Hecke, for £52m from Brighton, Marcos Senesi, Andrew Robertson and Martin Dubravka.

With so many new signings and different managers, who knows what to expect?

Dastan Satpaev is attempting to become the first Kazakh player to appear in a Premier League match.

Quick, sharp in the box and relatively small in stature, Satpaev is stylistically often compared to former Argentina and Manchester City striker Sergio Aguero.

Asked whether he will get a chance at Chelsea this season amid talk of a potential loan move, Xabi Alonso said: "We still have to take decisions.

"I knew Dastan from Almaty," added Alonso, who faced the player with his former club Real Madrid last season.

"He is a ball threat, he attacks the inner channel well and is good as a striker coming from the outside.

"He is really strong, really quick and I have been really impressed with him."

title: The FA confirm 3 new anti-timewasting rules
description: The FA have confirmed that the International Football Association Board have approved a new goalkeeper injury trial for the 2026/27 Premier League season.Photo by Michael Regan/Getty ImagesThe FA have...
fullText:
The FA have officially announced that English football has received approval from IFAB to trial a new system to cut down on tactical goalkeeper injury timeouts.

For a while, teams have abused the fact that a goalkeeper going down for medical treatment doesn’t have to leave the field of play afterwards. A goalkeeper can go down, disrupt momentum, and give their team time to address things tactically during the break, with no negative consequences.

The trial will introduce such a consequence, requiring the head coach to immediately nominate a player to leave the pitch for a minimum of one minute after the game restarts.

There will be exceptions to the rule, including if the goalkeeper is fouled, if the goalkeeper is bleeding, or if the goalkeeper and an outfield player have collided and both need attention.

But the hope is that this will cut down on potential sporting advantages associated with such stoppages.

The FA add that they will also be introducing a five-second countdown option for match officials to use when they believe players are unfairly delaying a throw-in or goal-kick. The system was used at the World Cup, and it will now be introduced in English football.

Finally, a ten-second limit will be in place for players leaving the pitch when substituted.

The trial will take place across the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the League Cup this season, as well as the upcoming Community Shield match. So it will apply to Arsenal in all competitions except the Champions League.

title: 'Classic manipulative behaviour' or 'the last step' for Arsenal?
description: Like everyone else, I am transfixed by the transfers happening every day in the Premier League.  It helps to have a lot of money and a brand name that attracts the top players.  Manchester City come to mind right away.
fullText:
Like everyone else, I am transfixed by the transfers happening every day in the Premier League. There is always the temptation to make a snap judgement of what has happened in the market so far, but this is unfair.

There is so much business still to be done and so many difficulties to overcome. Clubs often have to be sure that money is coming in from sales before they can spend on new players.

The gold standard is those who know what they want and move early because they have had a plan in place all along. It helps to have a lot of money and a brand name that attracts the top players.

Manchester City come to mind right away. With Rodri injured and Bernardo Silva gone, the move for Elliot Anderson, even at £116m, seems obvious and sensible in hindsight. Even without Pep Guardiola they are still title favourites alongside Arsenal because of that methodology.

But the Gunners have moved sensibly over the summer so far. Piero Hincapie was a no-brainer, particularly as William Saliba is injured, but I'd expect one more cover player in that position. What I didn't expect was a story suggesting that Vinicius Junior might be tempted to north London.

I hate being 'played' in these circumstances. Is Vini Jr, his agent or indeed Real Madrid just using Arsenal as a bargaining chip in contract talks?

This would be classic manipulative behaviour but if the chips are cashed in, it'd be an incredible win for Mikel Arteta. The Brazilian's wages feel wrong for Arsenal, but his addition would make that last step to becoming European champions far more likely.

title: Zirkzee 'too good for role Man Utd want him to play'
description: Co-hosts Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed which players impressed them in Manchester United's comfortable pre-season win over Rosenborg in the latest episode of BBC Radio Manchester's The Devils' Advocate podcast. fullText:
Co-hosts Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed which players impressed them in Manchester United's comfortable pre-season win over Rosenborg in the latest episode of BBC Radio Manchester's The Devils' Advocate podcast.

Drinkwater was full of praise for Joshua Zirkzee, who scored a "Puskas award nominee" goal in the friendly, slaloming his way past defenders and goalkeeper before tapping into an empty net.

"It was a great goal and really nice to watch," he said.

"It did kind of look like United were playing on Fifa with the difficulty [level] set on amateur. It was so slow the way it happened and there's no way a goal like that would be scored in the Premier League, but I'm not saying that to discount Joshua Zirkzee or take anything away from him. It was a lovely goal."

On Zirkzee being linked with a move away from Old Trafford, Drinkwater added: "At times, he comes on and is the exact type of player you need in a game. I like a lot of his attributes and you can tell by the way he plays that he would do very well in the Italian league.

"He plays just a little bit slower but he is really, really good on the ball. He is so slick but he needs to play in a slower league.

"He's one of those players who is too good for the role we want him to play, which is very occasionally coming on and making an impact, and very rarely starting games. I wouldn't mind if we let him go."

title: Salah, Stones & Sancho - who are the Premier League free agents?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at some of the notable out-of-contract players who playing in the English top flight last season.
fullText:
The 2026-27 Premier League season is fast approaching but there are still plenty of players yet to secure their club futures.

Whether by choice or force, contracts have been run down and career paths changed.

BBC Sport takes a look at some of the notable out-of-contract players who were playing for a club in the English top flight last season.

John Stones, 32 (Last club: Manchester City)

Stones now left City after a decade at the club in which he won 15 major trophies. Picked for England by Thomas Tuchel despite recent injury issues, Stones has most recently been linked with former club Everton and Italian giants AC Milan.

Mohamed Salah, 33 (Last club: Liverpool)

Salah's last few months at Anfield were not easy as his relationship with boss Arne Slot appeared to disintegrate. Both have now left Liverpool. It was widely expected Salah would move to the Saudi Pro League once the World Cup was over but he has since been linked with a move to Turkish club Besiktas.

Jadon Sancho, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

It has been a turbulent few years for Sancho since joining United from Borussia Dortmund for £73m in 2021 and he has spent the last two and-a-half years playing elsewhere on loan, most recently at Aston Villa following a lacklustre period at Chelsea. Sancho made just 30 Premier League appearances for United but has reportedly received an offer from Qatari side Al-Rayyan.

Yves Bissouma, 29 (Last club: Tottenham Hotspur)

Mali midfielder Bissouma made just 11 top-flight appearances last season as he struggled with injury and off-field issues at Spurs. He is reportedly keen on staying in the Premier League, with Fulham said to be interested.

Stefan Ortega, 33 (Last club: Nottingham Forest)

Former Manchester City number two goalkeeper Ortega made 10 appearances across all competitions for Forest last season. A move to Greek side Olympiacos is potentially close.

Tyrell Malacia, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

A difficult four-year spell at United for the Dutch left-back was marred by injuries and long stints on the sidelines. A chronic knee issue requiring surgery kept him out for over 500 days, causing him to miss the entire 2023–24 campaign. He has made just 11 appearances across all competitions since.

Adama Traore, 30 (Last club: West Ham)

Traore was released by the Hammers in the wake of their relegation to the Championship after just six months at the club. The powerful Spanish winger has been linked with a move back to Wolves, where he spent five years.

description: Richard Hughes' summer transfer window last term was expected to change things for Liverpool.He spent over £450 million on new players in an attempt to help the Reds retain their Premier League title...
fullText:
Richard Hughes' summer transfer window last term was expected to change things for Liverpool.

He spent over £450 million on new players in an attempt to help the Reds retain their Premier League title and potentially win the Champions League.

And, on paper, the additions of Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak promised to do exactly that but, for one reason or another, that isn't how things panned out.

They were knocked out in the round of 16 of the Champions League and they also only managed to finish in fifth place which, after their massive summer of spending, was far from ideal.

These poor performances led to fans demanding that new players were brought in and even made some of the Liverpool players decide they were better off elsewhere.

Of all the departures though, Mohamed Salah's is the one that has hit Liverpool the hardest and, no matter what Hughes tries to do, he can't seem to rectify it with another one of his disaster-classes feeling like it's about to arise.

Yan Diomande was the player who most Liverpool fans thought would be brought in to replace Salah.

Even before the summer transfer window opened, the Ivorian was being linked with an Anfield switch with Liverpool briefing most media outlets that he was their number one target.

In the end, however, Diomande chose against making a Liverpool switch and it was reported that he'd prefer his next move to be Paris Saint-Germain.

So, from then on, there was only really the Parisians being linked with a move but, since hardly any movement has been made regarding the deal, other clubs are starting to join the race and now, according to Fabrizio Romano, Real Madrid are 'in talks' with RB Leipzig about a potential move for the attacker.

"Manchester City have gone quiet on Yan Diomande days ago after calls to check the situation, same for Arsenal," he wrote.

"Diomande has only opened doors to Real Madrid since he agreed personal terms with Paris Saint-Germain in June.

"Real Madrid now in club to club talks with Leipzig."

fullText:
Chelsea are in talks to sign highly regarded set-piece coach Austin MacPhee from Aston Villa but face competition from other Premier League clubs as well as Saudi Pro League teams.

Villa would be due compensation for MacPhee with his contract understood to have a specified release clause.

The Scottish coach, 46, has combined his role at Villa Park with a similar position with the Portugal national team for the past five years under Roberto Martinez, who resigned after the World Cup.

Villa scored more goals from set-pieces than any other team in Europe's top five leagues during the 2023-24 season.

They followed that by ranking among the top five a season later and finished joint-top with Arsenal in the Premier League last season.

MacPhee would be one of a number of staff members to leave Villa Park this summer after helping the club win the Europa Conference League and qualify for the Champions League under manager Unai Emery.

New Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has space in his current backroom staff as previous set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who joined from Brentford for £750,000 in 2024, is moving away from a touchline role and into a more behind-the-scenes position.

Chelsea signed Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117m this week, with Alejandro Garnacho moving in the other direction on an initial loan that will likely become permanent through an option to buy.

title: Newcastle and Liverpool planning Keegan tribute at season opener
description: Newcastle United and Liverpool are in discussions over a tribute to Kevin Keegan before their Premier League opener at St James' Park on Sunday 23rd August.
fullText:
Newcastle United and Liverpool are in discussions over a tribute to Kevin Keegan before their Premier League opener at St James' Park.

Keegan, who died at the age of 75 this week, is revered at both clubs, having enjoyed legendary spells as a player with Liverpool and as both player and manager at Newcastle.

The two clubs are to face each other in the opening match of their 2026-27 season on Sunday, 23 August (16:30 BST).

Newcastle said in a statement that they are talking to Liverpool "to ensure [Keegan's] memory is marked fittingly before the game".

The club added they "will work closely with supporter groups... as well as the Premier League, to shape tributes".

Keegan spent two seasons as a Newcastle player from 1982 before returning as their manager in 1992 for the first of two spells in charge. He won three league titles, the European Cup, two Uefa Cups and the FA Cup during a trophy-laden six years at Liverpool.

Gifted, charismatic and passionate amid highs and lows - Keegan obituary

Newcastle's men's, women's and under-21 sides will wear black armbands during their pre-season matches to honour Keegan, who guided the club to Premier League promotion in 1992-93 and second place in the 1995-96 top flight.

A minute's silence will be observed before Eddie Howe's side play Gateshead in an away friendly this Saturday.

Keegan's photo will be displayed on screens at St James' Park in the seventh minute - a reference to the number seven shirt he wore as a player - when the men's side face Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg on 15 and 16 August.

The same tribute will take place when the women's team face Inter Milan on 16 August, giving supporters the chance to join a minute's applause for the former England captain and manager.

Newcastle said they will consult Keegan's family on plans for a permanent tribute.

In June, Keegan had revealed he had stage four cancer, which is the most advanced stage of cancer and means the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

His family initially disclosed he was battling the disease in January.

A statement on behalf of the Keegan family this week said he was "surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments".

During an illustrious playing career, he also enjoyed spells at Scunthorpe United, Hamburg and Southampton before managing Newcastle, Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Tzolis’ move to the Emirates Stadium – Arsenal’s third permanent transfer of the close season – came 48 hours after the north Londoners missed out on Morgan Rogers who signed a £117 million British-record fee with Chelsea, describing his new employers as the “biggest club in London.”

Tzolis scored 43 times in 108 appearances for Club Brugge, and lined up in the Belgians’ 3-0 Champions League defeat to Mikel Arteta’s side last season.

Arsenal’s sporting director Andrea Berta said in a statement on Thursday: “We’re delighted to have completed the signing of Christos Tzolis.

“Christos is an extremely versatile attacking player who naturally operates on the left but is comfortable across the front line. He’s an excellent finisher with both feet, thrives in tight spaces, and possesses incredible technical ability.

“Christos has produced outstanding numbers in terms of goals and assists over the last three seasons, and he’s a player who will raise the technical level of our squad, while bringing positive energy, enthusiasm, and a strong mentality to our team.

“We’re confident Christos will make a significant contribution to our club, and we hope our supporters will enjoy watching him play in an Arsenal shirt. We look forward to sharing this exciting new chapter together.”

Tzolis played 14 Premier League games for Norwich during the 2021-22 campaign but did not find the back of the net. Loan periods with FC Twente and Fortuna Dusseldorf followed before he made the move to Club Brugge in 2024.

Tzolis follows Piero Hincapie – who turned his temporary deal with Arsenal into a full-time switch – and goalkeeper Illan Meslier, a free signing from Leeds, as the Gunners’ third signing.

The announcement arrives as a boost of sorts for Arteta after defender William Saliba was this week ruled out for an “extensive period” with a back problem which curtailed his World Cup. The France international is set to miss the start of Arsenal’s Premier League defence.

title: Will Man United sign Aurelien Tchouameni? Why Real Madrid midfielder now looks like attainable transfer target
description: Aurelien Tchouameni had looked likely to sign a new Real Madrid contract. Suddenly, a move to the Premier League is back on the table.
fullText:
Will Man United sign Aurelien Tchouameni? Why Real Madrid midfielder now looks like attainable transfer target originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Another year, another transfer window where Manchester United attempt to sign midfielders.

Except this time, they're actually getting them.

Michael Carrick made it clear that strengthening the heart of the team was a priority, and they have already brought in Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. Their next target would appear to be Aurelien Tchouameni of Real Madrid.

Rumours of interest in Tchouameni surfaced before the 2026 World Cup, but nothing really came of it. However, recent reports indicate United's interest never really went away and, in fact, they may now be in a stronger position to strike what would likely be one of the biggest deals of the window — perhaps one that even rivals the fee Chelsea paid for Morgan Rogers.

Could it actually happen? Let's look at the latest.

MORE:Man United's preseason schedule as Michael Carrick aims for strong start

The Sun's Samuel Luckhurst reported on July 23 that Madrid may now consider selling Tchouameni to Man United, despite previous indications that they would resist all but the most outlandish bids.

United are known to want another midfielder, ideally one that is a specialist defensive player, despite signing Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Tielemans from Aston Villa. The Red Devils' priority is a No. 6 in the approximate age range of 22-26, and ideally one with plenty of top-level experience already. Tchouameni, a La Liga, Champions League and Club World Cup winner who has played at two World Cups for France, fits the bill.

There is a long way to go before this can be considered very likely to happen, but the chances of a deal being struck would seem to be higher than they were a month ago.

It was previously reported that Madrid were eager to keep Tchouameni, and talk even emerged that he had agreed to a contract extension. Now, however, The Sun says the Spanish club would be prepared to listen to offers.

Madrid have already brought in Bernardo Silva on a free transfer and have Federico Valverde and Eduardo Camavinga on the books. It is also believed they are making every effort to sign Manchester City midfielder Rodri, who has a year left on his contract but appears keen to return to Spain.

🚨 Excl. - Agreement in principle for a contract until 2030 between #Rodri and #RealMadrid, which are ready to open talks to try to sign him from #ManchesterCity. #MCFC would like to keep him and offered the contract extension, but the midfielder has not accepted. #transfers

— Nicolò Schira (@NicoSchira) July 23, 2026

Arda Guler and Jude Bellingham are also capable of playing as part of a midfield pivot if required, so selling Tchouameni to balance the books and reduce squad bloating would make sense, even if new coach Jose Mourinho would be happy if he stayed. Madrid could also make further additions in this window if they can command a big enough transfer fee for the France international.

Few concrete figures have been suggested when it comes to United and Tchouameni, partly because no formal transfer bid has yet been submitted.

There was a report from Miguel Serrano just prior to the World Cup that Madrid would only listen to offers of around £153.4m ($205.7m), but it is unlikely the Red Devils would sanction such an exorbitant spend on a 26-year-old with two years left on his contract.

Madrid paid £72.5m ($89.7m) for Tchouameni to sign him from Monaco in 2022, so they would want at least to recoup that sum in full. An offer in the region of £90m ($120m) guaranteed might get negotiations to advance.

Tchouameni was allegedly involved in a "very serious" altercation with teammate Federico Valverde at Madrid's training ground in early May 2026.

Reports at the time indicated that matters escalated to the point of a fight between the two, during which Valverde slipped and banged his head on a table. The Uruguayan was later treated in hospital.

The club fined both players €500,000, but Valverde issued a statement insisting the incident had been blown out of proportion. Tchouameni, while not denying that some sort of altercation occurred, dismissed the "huge reaction" in the media, adding: "A lot of nonsense was said in the press."

United have made three signings to date in this transfer window: goalkeeper Karl Darlow, and midfielders Tielemans and Santos.

Darlow was a free transfer after his contract at Leeds United expired. He was brought in to provide additional goalkeeping depth, with Andre Onana having returned to Trabzonspor on loan and Altay Bayindir expected to be sold.

Tielemans and Santos cost a combined £83m ($110.8m) in initial fees. United have not yet sold any players to offset the expense, but they did earn £10.57m ($14.1m) as part of a clause in Mason Greenwood's Marseille contract. Greenwood was sold by the French club to Fenerbahce this window.

title: Pandur joined Rangers after Hull planned new number one
description: New Rangers goalkeeper Ivor Pandur says he passed up the chance to be part of Hull City's return to the Premier League after being told they planned to sign a new number one this summer.
fullText:
New Rangers goalkeeper Ivor Pandur has revealed he passed up the chance to be part of Hull City's return to the Premier League after being told they planned to sign a new number one this summer.

The 26-year-old, who was part of Croatia's squad at the World Cup, arrived at Ibrox at the same time as former England cap Jack Butland made the opposite journey to be part of Sergej Jakirovic's squad.

"It's strange," Pandur, who made 48 appearances last season as Hull won promotion via the play-offs, said. "The gaffer is also Croatian like me. He told me he wanted me to stay and to play.

"But the club had a different idea of bringing in another keeper who has Premier League experience, which I don't have yet.

"So they made it clear for me to know there would be somebody coming in as a number one.

"Whether I agree with it or not, it doesn't matter. That's football.

"I'm just proud and happy I got to share those two and a half years at the club with all these great people. It means everything to me."

Rangers' interest in Pandur, who said it was "a lovely experience" to play in front of the crowd at Ibrox for the first time in Wednesday's pre-season friendly win over St Etienne, began before he joined Hull from Fortuna Sittard in 2024.

"I remember my agent was talking to a director who is not with this club any more and it came close," he recalled.

"It is probably better because I am much better than I was three or four years ago - I have developed quite a lot and there's still more to come and I think I'm in a perfect place to improve."

Pandur revealed that contact with Rangers "was ongoing through the season" but that "I didn't have much to think about" when the approach came and a deal was done "in a couple of days".

His arrival at Ibrox coincides with the return of former number one Allan McGregor as goalkeeping coach.

"It means a lot to me to have him as my coach," Pandur said. "It is up to me to learn from him and ask him questions and develop under him.

"He is a legend of the club and also in Europe he played a lot of games and in the national team as well.

"When I found he was the goalkeeping coach, it just filled me with happiness. I want to learn from the best and that's why I came as well."

Pandur had consulted Hull team-mates John Lundstram and Kieran Dowell, and former Rangers striker Antonio Colak, before making his decision.

"They told me they demand a lot," he revealed. "There is pressure. They want trophies.

"I want all of that as well, so I never ran from pressure, from responsibility all my career - it's just the way I've been raised.

"I want to test myself on the biggest stage and I think Rangers are one of the biggest clubs in Europe. In my mind I know I'm ready for it."

title: Jeff Bezos Reportedly Might Join Bid for Liverpool Stake
description: A deal could value the Premier League club at roughly $6 billion.
fullText:
A group led by the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal is in talks to buy a minority stake in Premier League soccer team Liverpool from Fenway Sports Group—and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos reportedly may join the bid.

FSG, which in addition to Liverpool owns the Red Sox and backs the PGA Tour’s for-profit commercial entity, confirmed on Tuesday there are discussions with a group led by Amit Bhatia, son-in-law of Lakshmi Mittal, about a “strategic minority investment” in Liverpool. The Mittal family, which includes Aditya Mittal—a Celtics minority owner who just lost out on buying the Seahawks to a group led by 49ers minority owner Vinod Khosla—is also part of the group (Aditya is Lakshmi’s son).

A deal could value Liverpool at around $6 billion, the Financial Times reported.

After that news came out, Sky News reported that Bezos has “held discussions” about joining the consortium, although the report cautioned there is no guarantee he will end up investing. Representatives for two of Bezos’s companies, Amazon and Blue Origin, did not respond to requests for comment (Bezos also owns the Washington Post).

Although he has yet to wade into the world of sports ownership, Bezos’s name often comes up when teams are for sale given his deep pockets (he is the world’s fourth-richest person with a net worth of almost $254 billion, according to Forbes). As examples, he was linked to the Commanders in 2021, before they ultimately sold to Josh Harris for $6.05 billion, and his name came up when the Celtics were for sale (although a source close to Bezos later denied his interest).

Bhatia, who for the last 18 seasons has co-owned the EFL Championship’s Queens Park Rangers, stepped down from the team’s board on Tuesday and agreed to “transfer” his stake in the club to majority owner Ruben Gnanalingam. The statement announcing his departure did not mention the potential Liverpool bid.

A source familiar with the matter tells Front Office Sports that discussions with the Bhatia-led group are preliminary and there is no guarantee a deal will be reached. If a deal does happen, it would not be the first time FSG has sold a minority stake in Liverpool; in 2023, private-equity firm Dynasty Equity acquired a minority stake in the soccer club.

Harsh Talikoti of investment bank Houlihan Lokey tells FOS that the reported $6 billion valuation “underlines how far premium sports franchises have moved from trophy assets to institutional-grade investments.”

“Scarcity is the defining feature,” Talikoti said. “Clubs like Liverpool, with more than 130 years of history, 20 English league titles, six European Cups and a genuinely global fanbase, simply cannot be replicated, and their diversified revenues across media rights, matchday and commercial partnerships make them attractive to long-term capital.”

That the Bhatia group is eyeing a minority stake also underscores a growing trend in pro sports. Vinod Khosla, who just bought the Seahawks, owns a minority stake in the 49ers that he will have to divest before his deal for Seattle can be completed. David Tepper, who in 2018 bought the Panthers, was previously a minority investor in the Steelers. Leagues like the NFL generally view potential majority owners more favorably if they are first minority owners, because those minority deals require due diligence that makes it easier for people to be vetted once they’re trying to become majority owners, multiple sources have told FOS.

Another reason the Bhatia-led group may be appealing to the Premier League is that the Mittal family has been building a portfolio of sports investments that shows they can be good stewards of franchises. In addition to Aditya Mittal’s $1 billion minority investment in the Celtics, the family’s patriarch, Lakshmi Mittal, purchased the Rajasthan Royals of the Indian Premier League in May for $1.65 billion.

Talikoti said it’s “telling” that the interest in Liverpool comes from a “family with an established sports portfolio,” which represents a “sign of capital converging across leagues on the same underlying thesis.”

“Minority stakes have become the preferred entry point, letting investors gain exposure to that growth story while incumbent owners retain control and crystallize value,” Talikoti added.

Editors’ note: RedBird Capital Partners owns a stake in Fenway Sports Group. RedBird IMI, in which RedBird Capital Partners is a joint venture partner, is the primary investor in Front Office Sports.

In Marcus Rashford's case, there are a limited number of clubs globally who could match his current salary. And where a club are interested, the player has to want to join them.

Judging by his recent social media post, he would not do anything to jeopardise his England place.

BBC Sport has also been told of some Premier League clubs he would not be keen to move to.

So where will Rashford be when the transfer window closes on 1 September? Currently, the likeliest answer, by some distance, is Manchester United.

After that: Any Spanish club, any Turkish club, any German club. The vagueness there underlines the current lack of market for the 15th highest scorer in United's history, with 138 goals - someone who is only 17 short of a place in the top 10.

There are plenty, including former captain Gary Neville, who feel Rashford's time at Old Trafford is over and there should be no reconciliation.

In the end though, it may have to happen - and not everyone would be disappointed.

"A fit and focused Marcus Rashford has the ability to be one of the best players," said Rashford's friend Sam Smith - the Wrexham forward who scored the winner in their pre-season victory over Carrick's team in Helsinki on Saturday - when speaking to the United We Stand podcast.

"He has had a difficult time at United and getting away from it all was a good thing.

"I don't know what is going to happen but as his friend, I hope he comes back and proves how good a player he was, how good he can be and starts scoring goals again."

Arsenal, Manchester United, Tottenham, Manchester City and Chelsea have an interest in Scott.

BBC Sport reported in June that Arsenal had an approach for Scott turned down by Bournemouth.

The 22-year-old, who joined Bournemouth from Bristol City in 2023 for £25m, has two years left on his current deal with the Premier League side.

Bournemouth remain steadfast in their position that Scott is not for sale, despite him rejecting the contract offer that had been on the table for at least two months.

Bournemouth have insisted publicly, directly to the player and to interested clubs that he will remain on the south coast, even on his current contract.

That stance has been consistent and, despite talk of an £80m valuation, they have continued to reject approaches.

The south coast club are under no pressure to sell after qualifying for the Europa League and generating significant income through the sales last summer of Dean Huijsen, Milos Kerkez, Illia Zabarnyi and Dango Outtara.

They have taken a similar stance with highly rated forward Junior Kroupi, who is attracting interest from Arsenal and Tottenham.

Brazil international Rayan is also not expected to leave and has given no indication that he wants to, having only joined the club in January.

title: Why are Premier League transfer fees soaring?
description: With Morgan Rogers set to become the third £100m-plus Premier League transfer of the summer, BBC Sport looks at how the market keeps growing.
fullText:
Thirty-four years ago a £13m transfer caused national outrage in Italy.

When AC Milan signed Gianluigi Lentini from Torino in 1992 for a then world record fee, newspapers called the deal "obscene", while the Vatican's official newspaper described it as "an offence against the dignity of work".

Today that fee would barely register among the Premier League's biggest transfers.

This summer alone Chelsea have agreed a club record £117m deal for Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Manchester City paid Nottingham Forest £116m for Elliot Anderson, and Tottenham spent a club record £100m on Sandro Tonali.

These are not the only major deals. Tottenham also agreed an £85m move for West Ham midfielder Mateus Fernandes, Barcelona paid £69m to sign Anthony Gordon from Newcastle United, and Manchester United spent £50m on Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos.

It is the first transfer window in Premier League history to produce three £100m-plus signings - and there are still weeks to go before deadline day on 1 September.

During the 2025 summer window English top-flight clubs spent a record £3bn.

So why are transfer fees continuing to climb? Why are clubs paying record sums for players already playing in England? And why are more clubs willing to sell some of their biggest stars?

Rogers' move perhaps best encapsulates how today's market works

Chelsea are buying a player from Villa, who have finished above them in three of the past four seasons. Traditionally, clubs might have been reluctant to strengthen a direct rival in those circumstances.

Instead, Chelsea simply met Villa's valuation.

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire says one record fee quickly influences the next.

"It sets a benchmark," he says. "Forest wanted to be close to the record level because they felt Elliot Anderson was a critical player, a player very much in demand.

"We've then seen that surpassed by the Morgan Rogers fee - only slightly - but it allows the club to say, 'This is the record English signing'. So there's an element of bragging rights involved."

After City's £116m move for Anderson established a new market rate, Villa made it clear any club wanting Rogers would need to exceed that figure. Chelsea did exactly that, agreeing a guaranteed £117m fee.

Arsenal, who had identified Rogers as one of their leading targets, explored a deal but refused to meet Villa's asking price.

The episode shows how quickly the market can move. Once a new benchmark is established, comparable players inevitably see their valuations rise.

Part of the answer lies in supply and demand.

Premier League clubs must register at least eight homegrown players in their 25-man squads, while clubs competing in Uefa competitions must also satisfy homegrown quotas. That creates fierce competition for a relatively small pool of players capable of performing consistently at the highest level.

Buying domestically also removes many of the uncertainties associated with overseas recruitment.

Maguire describes Premier League players as "oven-ready".

"Because the Premier League is so wealthy, it's relatively rare that a club is in financial straits where it has to sell," he says.

"In the case of English players, you've then got the homegrown rule, which gives clubs more flexibility.

"You put all of those factors together and it means the Premier League is a big driver."

Clubs know how these players perform against top opposition, and understand they can cope with the physical demands of the Premier League and avoid many of the adaptation risks attached to recruiting from abroad.

That certainty carries a premium. So too does the Premier League's financial strength. Lucrative broadcasting revenues give English clubs spending power unmatched elsewhere in world football, allowing selling clubs to demand higher fees from domestic rivals than they might receive from overseas buyers.

Perhaps the more surprising trend has been clubs allowing key players to leave.

Villa have sold Rogers despite his importance under Unai Emery, while Forest accepted City's offer for Anderson. Newcastle sanctioned Gordon's move despite the England winger becoming one of Eddie Howe's most influential attacking players.

Such decisions reflect commercial strategy as much as football.

Major transfer fees create opportunities to strengthen several areas of a squad rather than relying on one star player, while major sales also provide greater flexibility.

Why are Man City breaking the bank for Anderson?

Those sales have also reignited debate about whether the Premier League's financial regulations place greater pressure on ambitious clubs outside the traditional biggest spenders to sell valuable assets.

Some argue that the rules favour clubs with the greatest financial resources, which are better placed to absorb record transfer fees.

The latest changes are also shaping how clubs approach the transfer market.

Maguire says financial regulations can influence transfer decisions, although he cautions that they are not always the decisive factor.

"Financial regulations might be a driving force, but not necessarily," he says.

"Because clubs don't have to sell from a financial point of view, it means they can extract maximum value from their players."

Villa's sale of Rogers and Forest's decision to cash in on Anderson have become part of that wider discussion, highlighting how regulation now shapes recruitment and squad building across the Premier League.

Rather than viewing these deals simply as losing important players, clubs now see them as opportunities to reshape their squads.

Whether those replacements prove as successful is another matter.

This summer has also brought a significant regulatory change.

The Premier League is transitioning away from profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) towards a new financial framework centred on squad-cost ratio (SCR) and sustainability and systemic resilience (SSR).

Rather than focusing primarily on rolling three-year losses, the new framework places greater emphasis on the relationship between football-related spending and revenue.

title: 'Newcastle were blessed to have him' - your memories of Keegan
description: John: He was the greatest English player of his generation and Newcastle were blessed to have him as a player at the end of his career in the 80s, and as an inspirational manager in the 90s.  King Kev was a special person who won the hearts of an adoring Geordie nation, and took us to the brink of winning the Premier League in the 1995-96 season.  Ali: I was lucky enough to get a ticket for King Kev's final game at Newcastle when the helicopter landed on the pitch and took him away after the celebrations.
fullText:
We asked for your memories of Newcastle legend Kevin Keegan after the sad news of his passing was announced on Monday.

Here are some of your replies and stories:

John: He was the greatest English player of his generation and Newcastle were blessed to have him as a player at the end of his career in the 80s, and as an inspirational manager in the 90s. King Kev was a special person who won the hearts of an adoring Geordie nation, and took us to the brink of winning the Premier League in the 1995-96 season. He inspired the players and fans to dream and achieve greatness, and is undoubtedly a legend who will live long in our hearts and minds. He deserves a statue and a stand naming after him. RIP King Kev.

Ali: I was lucky enough to get a ticket for King Kev's final game at Newcastle when the helicopter landed on the pitch and took him away after the celebrations. I was a young teenager at the time and couldn't believe how many grown men around me were crying when the helicopter took off. He was absolutely loved and worshipped.

Ashley: I met Kevin a couple of times, he was always pleasant and happy to chat and give his time to those who had come to see him. He was the reason I fell in love with football and became a Newcastle fan. He truly got the club going in the right direction and even though we didn't win a trophy with him, I would not change it. Thank you King Kev and rest easy.

Colin: What an amazing man! Big heart, took the city to heart. Brought so much happiness and joy to my family! Rest in peace.

Hugo: After watching him score his first goal, on debut, for Newcastle from the Gallowgate End in to which he slotted the ball, I won a competition to play football with Kevin Keegan when he was a Newcastle player. He gifted me a signed copper print of that goal that I still treasure today. Legend.

Sandra: A great player, I was thrilled and proud when he became Newcastle's manager and got us so close to winning the league title. A Geordie legend and a great loss to football.

Jonny: Met him and the whole Newcastle squad in a departure lounge at Newcastle Airport in 1993 on my way to a school skiing trip aged 11. All my classmates had gone round the squad getting autographs and photos but I was running late and last to arrive, so by the time I got to them most of the players had packed up and were moving on. He made them all come back into the room to sign for me because he didn't want me to be the only kid jetting off without a bag full of autographs. It's not just the football he was loved for.

Gary: He was the modern Newcastle United. A generation fell in love with football and the club because of him. He saved the club, he saved us. I don't think you can ever underestimate the impact he had on Tyneside and its people. He may never have delivered the silverware but he gave us hope. He let us dream and that's what football should be.

title: 'A special manager' - your memories of Keegan
description: John: I have great memories of Kevin Keegan's Championship title promotion season, establishing City in the Premier League, and of his tremendous impact on the direction and ambition of the entire club during his time as manager. fullText:
We asked for your memories of former Manchester City manager Kevin Keegan after the sad news of his passing was announced on Monday.

Here are some of your replies and stories:

John: I have great memories of Kevin Keegan's Championship title promotion season, establishing City in the Premier League, and of his tremendous impact on the direction and ambition of the entire club during his time as manager. A true great as a player, and a special manager who did so much to revive sleeping giants, Newcastle, Fulham and Manchester City. Rest in peace, King Kevin.

Colin: Kevin Keegan, what a man! Would we have all the current success if he hadn't brought his entertaining brand of football to City? People may see his period as City manager as a footnote in his wonderful career, but his four years at City were as entertaining as it gets. Thank you, King Kev.

Keith: His City teams were amongst the most exciting I have ever seen, and he could clearly attract excellent players. The football was sometimes so attacking, it was bonkers and NEVER dull. That 2001-02 second tier campaign was so memorable... Ali Bernabia, Eyal Berkovic, Shaun Goater, Darren Huckerby, Stuart Pearce. Rest in peace, Kevin, thank you for your time at City.

John: RIP King Kev - Thank you for the great memories from your time as Manchester City manager.

Chris: True legend, great player and wore his heart on a sleeve.

fullText:
Sport Bild reports that Freiburg keeper Noah Atubolu will remain absent from Freiburg team training camp ahead of his move to the Premier League. Atubolu’s move away from the Bundesliga has long been a forgone conclusion. Freiburg immediately procured a replacement for their soon-to-depart player (Werder Bremen’s Mio Backhaus) almost immediately after the 2025/26 Bundesliga concluded.

Sport Bild nevertheless has some new news to offer on Atubolu’s impending departure. The 24-year-old is evidently so intent on heading to the Premier League that he has turned down interest from Juventus. Insofar as which Premier League club Atubolu will end up with, the field has been narrowed to two.

Sport Bild claims that Atubolu has already turned down offers from Premier League newcomers Hull City AFC and Coventry City FC, as he prefers to join a club in England that is considered to be more established. Aston Villa (who have already signed Atubolu’s Freiburg teammate Johan Manzambi) and Bournemouth (now coached by German Marco Rose) appear the two most likely clubs to secure Atubolu’s services.

Thirty-four years ago a £13m transfer caused national outrage in Italy.

When AC Milan signed Gianluigi Lentini from Torino in 1992 for a then world record fee, newspapers called the deal "obscene", while the Vatican's official newspaper described it as "an offence against the dignity of work".

Today that fee would barely register among the Premier League's biggest transfers.

This summer alone Chelsea have agreed a club record £117m deal for Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Manchester City paid Nottingham Forest £116m for Elliot Anderson, and Tottenham spent a club record £100m on Sandro Tonali.

It is the first transfer window in Premier League history to produce three £100m-plus signings - and there are still weeks to go before deadline day on 1 September.

During the 2025 summer window English top-flight clubs spent a record £3bn.

So why are transfer fees continuing to climb? Why are clubs paying record sums for players already playing in England? And why are more clubs willing to sell some of their biggest stars?

Rogers' move perhaps best illustrates how today's market works.

Chelsea are buying a player from Villa, who have finished above them in three of the past four seasons. Traditionally, clubs might have been reluctant to strengthen a direct rival in those circumstances.
